intro: Alborada del gracioso, marked Assez vif, is the fourth piece of Ravel’s Miroirs: a dawn song for a Spanish jester, with guitar-like strumming on the piano between the verses. An unaccompanied melodic line interrupts the dance.

sections.label: A · Assez vif, guitar-like chords
sections.mNote: Tightly rolled chords and repeated notes set the dance rhythm.

sections.label: B · Plus lent, solo melody
sections.mNote: Plus lent: an unaccompanied melody alternates with strummed chords.

sections.label: Link · Repeated A in the bass
sections.mNote: The dance rhythm returns over a repeated A in the bass.

sections.label: A′ · Dry chords over E♭
sections.mNote: The opening strummed chords return at ppp in a new key.

sections.label: Coda · Staccato chords accelerating to D major
sections.mNote: Quiet chords accelerate towards the D-major ending.

cues.title: Opening, guitar-style chords
cues.text: The title means a dawn song of a jester. The piano opens with tightly rolled chords, marked sec, imitating a strummed guitar, with sharp bass notes beneath. The dance is in 6/8, and Ravel repeatedly interrupts its rhythm.
cues.evidence: Miroirs, Demets edition (1906), p. 31: Assez vif, mf sec, les arpèges très serrés. Guitar imitation and the title: https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329. Score: https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs,DemetsEd.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeated-note passage
cues.text: The right hand plays a rapidly repeated note, with short scales running off from it. The left hand keeps to a spare accompaniment below.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 33–34: rapid repeated-note passages and short scales; the technique is described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recitative, Plus lent
cues.text: The dance stops under a fermata. A single melodic line follows, Plus lent and expressif en récit, with the left hand silent. Strummed chords interrupt it repeatedly at the original tempo.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 35: fermata, Plus lent, 3/4 recitative and alternating 1er Mouvement chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ravel on the gracioso
cues.text: Ravel explained that his clown, the gracioso, was humorous but had an edge to him, and was less well meaning than Beaumarchais’s Figaro. Roger Nichols noted that the drier tone and lighter action of the Érard pianos Ravel favoured would sharpen the “guitar” chords.
cues.evidence: Roger Nichols’s note for Hyperion CDA67731/2 (2011) reports Ravel’s explanation of the clown’s character and makes the point about Érard pianos: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W5434_67731

cues.title: Dedication to Calvocoressi
cues.text: Ravel dedicated this movement to Calvocoressi, a critic and musicologist in his circle of friends. In Miroirs, Calvocoressi received the Spanish jester and Ricardo Viñes the sad birds.
cues.evidence: Dedications and Calvocoressi’s profession: https://imslp.org/wiki/Miroirs,_M.43_(Ravel,_Maurice) and https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.

cues.title: Repeated A in the bass
cues.text: The song descends from its high chords and the bass holds A. Ravel writes sans ralentir, without slowing. The repeated note restores the pulse of the dance before the dry guitar chords return.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, p. 39, third and fourth systems: p expressif, then repeated A and sans ralentir.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the strummed chords
cues.text: The strummed chords return at ppp over E♭ in the bass, marked très sec et bien rythmé. Repeated notes and glissandos follow.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 39–40: ppp, très sec et bien rythmé, E♭ bass and subsequent glissandos. The E♭ return is also described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final section and close in D major
cues.text: Another dry chord stops under a fermata. Quiet staccato chords follow over low repeated notes, and the song does not return. The piano moves to a final rush to D major, played without slowing at the end.
cues.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 41–43: sec. fermata chord, pp staccato passage and final sans ralentir. The D-major close is described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ballets russes, London, 1919
cues.text: The Ballets russes danced Alborada, in Ravel’s orchestration, at London’s Alhambra Theatre in July 1919 as part of Les jardins d’Aranjuez, with Chabrier’s Menuet pompeux and Fauré’s Pavane. Paris had heard the orchestral version first, on 17 May 1919, under Rhené-Baton with the Pasdeloup Orchestra.
cues.evidence: Manuel Cornejo’s Maurice Ravel chronology (1919): 17 May, première of the orchestration of Alborada del gracioso, Rhené-Baton, Concerts Pasdeloup, Cirque d’hiver; 18 July, Ballets russes at London’s Alhambra Theatre, with Alborada on the programme: https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf. Roger Nichols, Ravel (2011), chronology: the Ballets russes perform the Menuet pompeux, Alborada del gracioso and Fauré’s Pavane as Les Jardins d’Aranjuez (full-text excerpt seen).

transitions.title: Fermata, then an unaccompanied line
transitions.how: The dance reaches a fortissimo chord and stops under a fermata. Ravel changes to 3/4 and Plus lent, and a single unaccompanied line enters, marked expressif en récit. Between its phrases the strummed chords return at 1er Mouvement.

transitions.title: The song descends to A
transitions.to: Link · Repeated A in the bass
transitions.how: The high chords marked ff très expressif descend into a softer phrase. The piano holds a repeated A, marked sans ralentir. The dance pulse resumes as the last notes of the song end.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 39, first four systems.

transitions.title: Bass moves from A to E♭
transitions.from: Link · Repeated A in the bass
transitions.how: The repeated A gets softer, and the bass then moves to E♭ beneath the returning guitar chords. Ravel marks the chords ppp and très sec et bien rythmé. The harmony moves on towards F♯ as the chords grow louder.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, pp. 39–40; E♭–F♯ route described at https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329.

transitions.title: Quiet chords after the fermata
transitions.to: Coda · Staccato chords accelerating to D major
transitions.how: The repeated-note passage ends on a fortissimo chord marked sec., held under a fermata. Quiet staccato chords follow, with low repeated notes in the left hand, and lead into the coda, which closes in D major.
transitions.evidence: Demets edition, p. 41, last two systems; D-major close on p. 43.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
